assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correcting the spherical aberration of electron lenses is a clear, concrete invention that took electron microscopy from roughly 0.2 nm to sub-angstrom resolution. It is the enabling instrument advance behind atomic-resolution imaging and spectroscopy of interfaces, defects, oxides and nanostructures across physics, chemistry and materials science. It fits the 'discovery or invention' criterion well and is not a lifetime-achievement case.
assessment.attribution: Rose supplied the theoretical design of the corrector, Haider built the hexapole corrector for the TEM, and Urban led the first demonstration on materials. This is a natural three-person configuration. I note that the credited names omit Ondrej Krivanek, who developed the quadrupole-octupole corrector for the STEM in parallel; I cannot add him under the protocol, but the allocation of credit between TEM and STEM correction is a real question.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed: commercial aberration-corrected instruments have been routine worldwide for about two decades and underpin a large body of published work. Recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the STEM-corrector line (Krivanek and collaborators) must be recognised alongside the TEM-corrector line, which the credited names cannot express.
My own field is electron microscopy, so I should discount my familiarity with this candidate and acknowledge a possible bias in its favour.
Whether the committee would regard this as physics rather than a methods advance better suited elsewhere; I have not verified prior prize history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, trap many neutral atoms in a Lamb-Dicke regime and reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is a clear invention with direct consequences for metrology, tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early strontium clocks; Ye's group drove the record precision and uncertainty and the many-body clock work. A two-person prize is clean. Contributions from other groups (for example Ytterbium lattice clocks and ion-clock competitors) are real but not decisive for the concept.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by multiple laboratories and national metrology institutes, with stable interpretation and steady improvement; timing is good.
uncertainties: Whether the committee will want to link this to frequency combs (already recognised in 2005) and to ion clocks, which would complicate the scope.
I am relying on my background knowledge for the exact accuracy records and have not independently verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, followed by the observation of edge transport in HgTe quantum wells, opened a new class of matter that became a central framework in condensed-matter physics and in materials research on spin-orbit and surface states. The discovery combines a specific theoretical prediction with a decisive experimental confirmation.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposals; Molenkamp's group with Zhang's theory team realised and measured the effect in HgTe. The credited names leave out Shoucheng Zhang (deceased) and Bernevig and Hughes, whose HgTe proposal was essential to the experimental discovery; this is an unresolved allocation issue, though Molenkamp is the experimental anchor.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature: confirmed by many groups and materials, and now a standard topic. Recognition is timely, and long overdue by some views.
uncertainties: The role of the HgTe theoretical proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and of early three-dimensional topological-insulator work is not represented in the credited names.
Whether the prize would be framed around the two-dimensional or three-dimensional topological insulator is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at magic twist angles in bilayer graphene, and Jarillo-Herrero's group observed correlated insulating and superconducting states at those angles. This launched the moire field, a broad, original and experimentally controllable platform for strongly correlated and topological physics, with a clear theory-experiment link.
assessment.attribution: The theory-to-experiment chain gives a coherent three-person structure. Others (for example Dean, Kim, Yacoby, and the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto earlier theory on twisted bilayers) made important contributions, and the share between Bistritzer-MacDonald and the experimental side is not obviously fixed.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups since 2018, but the interpretation of the correlated phases and superconductivity is still debated, so the field may be somewhat young for a prize.
uncertainties: The origin and pairing mechanism of the superconductivity remain unsettled.
Priority questions around earlier continuum-model theory and parallel experiments by other groups.
Sample-to-sample variability (twist-angle disorder) complicates the independence of the confirmations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Giant room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in crystalline MgO barrier junctions, predicted from coherent spin-dependent tunnelling in first-principles theory and then realised, transformed spintronics, magnetic sensors, read heads and MRAM. A discovery with a clear mechanism and large technological reach, though it builds on a field already recognised by the 2007 prize.
assessment.attribution: Butler and Mathon with coworkers predicted the effect; Yuasa and Parkin (with independent work at AIST and IBM) achieved the large experimental values in 2004. Others such as Djayaprawira and Mathon are not in the credited list and the theory share is uncertain. A three-person grouping is defensible but contested.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced, with industrial adoption confirming the physics. Interface structure and its microscopic characterisation by TEM were key to understanding it, which I know first-hand as a method.
uncertainties: Priority between the theoretical prediction and the two near-simultaneous experimental demonstrations.
Whether the committee sees the advance as sufficiently distinct from the earlier spintronics prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical coherence tomography is an invention that provides depth-resolved imaging of tissue with micrometre resolution and is now the standard of care in ophthalmology. It has very large lasting impact; its relation to physics is through low-coherence interferometry, which the committee may see as a medical-technology application.
assessment.attribution: The 1991 Science paper by Huang, Swanson, Fujimoto and colleagues established the method. Earlier low-coherence interferometry work by Fercher, Hitzenberger and others (not in the credited names) complicates priority, and the student-versus-supervisor balance is a matter to examine.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of clinical and engineering use and many independent confirmations. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether it falls within the physics prize remit or is better placed in another prize.
Earlier priority claims for low-coherence interferometry in the eye.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models in a controlled way: the Mott-insulator transition, fermionic Mott states and antiferromagnetic correlations, and the quantum gas microscope. This is a major conceptual and experimental advance in quantum simulation, with a well-defined theoretical origin in the Jaksch-Zoller proposal.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the lattice Hubbard mapping, Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition, and Esslinger's group demonstrated the fermionic case. Greiner is also decisive for the microscope, and the four credited names cannot all be included. Some of the theory credit also belongs to Jaksch and Cirac, who are not in this entry.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of repeated confirmation, but the ultimate scientific payoff in answering open Hubbard questions is still arriving, which makes timing partly open.
uncertainties: Which of Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger is the best experimental choice.
Overlap with other cold-atom prizes (1997, 2001) and with the Rydberg and quantum computing candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gives a controlled non-perturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons, capturing the Mott transition and, combined with band-structure methods, enabling quantitative materials calculations. It is a deep and lasting theoretical tool in condensed-matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimensional limit, Georges and Kotliar the mapping onto an impurity problem, and Kotliar the combination with electronic structure. Walter Metzner is not in the credited names, which limits the fairness of any configuration. Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt remains reasonable among the available names.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely applied, though the approximation is local and its limits are well known, with extensions (cluster methods) developing.
uncertainties: Credit for the infinite-dimension limit versus the impurity mapping.
A theoretical-tool prize rather than a prediction confirmed by experiment; the committee may weigh this differently.
